title: The cabin's cost
hook: he lists every expense of his cabin: 28 dollars and twelve and a half cents (Walden 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, new clothes, and the half of the sentence that matters: a new wearer of clothes. Your line was no new clothes. Did something get started with only what you had? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

Boards. Old bricks. Two secondhand windows. Nails, hinges and screws, a latch, a little chalk. In the middle of Walden, a book full of pond water and birdsong, Thoreau stops and prints a receipt. Line by line, he lists what his cabin cost him, and then adds it up, down to the half cent: twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents. It's an odd page to find among the pond water. It's also a candid one.
screen: `BOARDS, BRICKS, A LATCH.` → `A RECEIPT IN THE BOOK.` → `DOWN TO THE HALF CENT.`

segments.voice: First, a borrowed axe. Thoreau tells us he began by borrowing an axe, and that he gave it back sharper than he got it. The cabin starts with something lent, and returned in better shape. Second, the list. He builds mostly from used materials: boards from an old shanty, secondhand bricks and windows. He tells us what each thing cost, and he isn't embarrassed by how small the numbers are. He's proud of them. The chapter is called Economy, and he means it literally. Third, the real price. Here's the sentence that turns the receipt into philosophy: "the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run." Not dollars. Life. Hours of work, years of payments, the evenings spent earning what a thing requires. By that measure, a bigger house can be very expensive indeed, even if the bank approves it. Fourth, why it matters. Thoreau isn't saying everyone should live in a cabin. He's asking his readers to write their own receipt. A price tag says what a thing costs in money. It says nothing about what it costs in life. And it closes a week that moved from Emerson's long goodbye to Thoreau's workbench, his grief for John, the river trip, and then Walden's warnings about quiet desperation and new clothes. The last of those days keep circling one plain question, and the receipt puts it in ink. What is a life being exchanged for? Is it worth it?
screen: `A BORROWED AXE, RETURNED SHARPER.` · `A LIST OF USED THINGS.` · `THE COST IS LIFE.` · `WRITE YOUR OWN RECEIPT.` · then, large: `THE CABIN'S COST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list what you really need. Settle, and breathe out slowly. In your mind, start a short list. Not what you want. What you actually need to live well this week. A place to sleep. Food. A few people. Some quiet. Let the list stay short. Then notice one thing that isn't on it, something that's been costing you a lot of life lately, in hours or in worry. Just notice it. No verdict. The bell holds the time.
The cabin's cost. Thoreau's receipt in Walden, down to the half cent, and the idea under it: the true cost of a thing is the amount of life you exchange for it. Today's word.

Your line: what it cost. Today, before you buy or agree to something, ask once: what will this cost in life, not just money? And look back over this week: which day's line is still with you? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Some readers of Walden keep a simple record of what they spend, in money and in time, after Thoreau's own itemized account of building his cabin.
